title: Coral and the Cover
premise: Beatrix Blackwood, a sleep-ruined interpreter for a faltering peace delegation, notices that Flight 447 to Meridian has been erased from every system while still airborne — and the delegation's motorcade is rerouted directly into its path. As she pieces together why a passenger manifest matches names from her own buried past, she realizes the 'incident' that broke her sleep is the same operation now hunting her. To survive until the border checkpoint shifts change at dawn, Beatrix must trade the one secret worth killing for: proof of who ordered the flight erased — evidence hidden in her own inherited memory of that night. She gives it up not to the men with guns but to a young delegation aide she's come to love as family, buying their escape and burning her last claim to innocence.
about_author: Tamsin Pemberton is a former conference interpreter who spent a decade working border summits before turning to fiction full-time. She writes thrillers about people whose professional silence becomes the most dangerous thing they own.

chapters.title: The Hour That Isn't There
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Insomniac Beatrix works the final session of a doomed peace summit, translating threats she half-understands. A recurring 3:14 a.m. nightmare fragments through her day. Emotional beat: exhaustion masking dread; she senses the talks are theater for something worse.

chapters.title: Manifest of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Reviewing travel documents for the delegation, she finds Flight 447 listed on an itinerary no airline admits to. One passenger name stops her cold — it belongs to a man she saw die years ago. Beat: first crack in her controlled world.

chapters.title: Rerouted
chapters.summary: Delegation leader Ambassador Voss's POV. Security abruptly reroutes the motorcade toward a rural checkpoint 'for safety.' Voss suspects politics; Beatrix suspects the flight. Beat: unease hardening into certainty as the convoy leaves the city behind.

chapters.title: Every Record Gone
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. At a fuel stop she confirms it: Flight 447 has vanished from radar archives, booking systems, even news feeds — while witnesses swear it's still in the air. Beat: vertigo of unreality; her insomnia suddenly feels like preparation.

chapters.title: The Boy in Seat 12C
chapters.summary: Aide Tomas's POV, introducing him. Tomas, nineteen, quietly photographs everything, including a boy boarding 447 who resembles Beatrix. He doesn't know why he kept the photo. Beat: found-family seed planted; two watchers orbiting the same truth.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Meridian
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The convoy reaches the border post hours early; the shift change is at dawn and they must wait. Soldiers recognize something in the delegation's papers — or in her face. Beat: trap closing; nowhere left to be invisible.

chapters.title: What the Incident Was
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Beatrix's POV. Five years ago: an extraction gone wrong, a plane she interpreted aboard, a man shot mid-sentence, and the secret she swallowed to survive. Beat: the reader finally sees her wound; memory as inheritance.

chapters.title: Men Who Don't Ask Questions
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Plainclothes agents board the delegation's bus, polite and wrong. Tomas hides his camera card inside Beatrix's interpreter case without telling her. Beat: trust extended blindly; tension of shared secrets unshared.

chapters.title: Voss's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ambassador Voss's POV. Voss privately offers to hand over 'the interpreter' if the soldiers let the delegation cross. He believes Beatrix is expendable collateral. Beat: betrayal from within; the found family already has a fault line.

chapters.title: Overheard in Two Languages
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Interpreting between the soldiers' commander and Voss, Beatrix hears them discuss Flight 447 in coded logistics jargon — and her own codename. Beat: cold clarity; she was never a witness, she's the loose end.

chapters.title: The Card in the Case
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Agents search luggage; Tomas watches his hidden card pass inches from discovery. Beatrix covers for him instinctively, lying fluently in three languages. Beat: alliance sealed without words; fear transmuted into loyalty.

chapters.title: Dawn Shift Change
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The checkpoint rotates guards; a window opens for ninety minutes. But the new shift includes a man from her flashback — the shooter, older, decorated. Beat: past and present collide; escape route and executioner are the same door.

chapters.title: Ninety Minutes
chapters.summary: Alternating Beatrix/Tomas POV. They slip the compound during the change, moving through fog toward a freight depot where 447 reportedly landed. Beat: breathless momentum; first time Beatrix acts instead of endures.

chapters.title: The Hangar of the Vanished
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Inside the hangar: the plane, intact, passengers' belongings neatly catalogued — including the dead man's briefcase addressed to her. Beat: horror of bureaucratic evil; the flight wasn't lost, it was filed away.

chapters.title: Inheritance of Evidence
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The briefcase holds records naming everyone who ordered the erasure — and revealing Beatrix's testimony five years ago was buried, not ignored. Her 'secret' could topple the network. Beat: her shame reframed as power; grief turning to resolve.

chapters.title: The Shooter's Sermon
chapters.summary: Antagonist Colonel Reyes's POV. Reyes corners Beatrix, offering absolution and death in the same breath: give back the case, sleep again, forget. Beat: temptation articulated; the villain speaks her own exhaustion back to her.

chapters.title: What Beatrix Trades
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Surrounded, she negotiates: she'll surrender the case — after handing Tomas a copy and the truth, making him her heir. Beat: climax pivot; she chooses transmission over survival, family over self.

chapters.title: Runway Fire
chapters.summary: Action climax, alternating POVs. The hangar burns; Reyes dies pursuing the copy rather than the woman; Beatrix and Tomas cross the airfield under the shifting checkpoint lights as 447 finally 'reappears' in the world's systems. Beat: catharsis through chaos.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. At a neutral embassy she gives, in four languages, the statement she swallowed five years ago. It costs her the career, the immunity, the anonymity. Beat: sacrifice completed; sleeplessness beginning to lift.

chapters.title: The Boy from 12C
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The boy from the flight — the dead man's son — meets Beatrix. She can't return his father, only the truth and a place to stay. Beat: found family formalized in loss; tenderness after violence.

chapters.title: First Sleep
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Weeks later, in a borrowed house near the sea, Beatrix sleeps through the night and wakes disoriented by peace. News breaks that the buried records surfaced via 'an anonymous archive.' Beat: quiet resolution; the body finally believing it's safe.

chapters.title: Coral and the Cover
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Beatrix's POV. She and Tomas visit the reef where she once scattered the dead man's ashes; coral grows over what was hidden, alive over the covered. She begins interpreting again — this time for refugees, on the record. Beat: inheritance transformed; memory kept, not buried.
